The following text is from Ruth Okafor's 1998 memoir about her years as a vaccination nurse.

Every morning before dawn I packed the clinic cooler: vials of measles vaccine, boxes of syringes, ice packs wrapped in newspaper. When spring rains washed out the road to the hill villages, I walked the last mile with the cooler strapped to my back. <u>It always weighed more than anything inside it, because every name on my list was a child waiting at the end of that road.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains that the cooler was built of heavy materials that made it hard to carry.
It conveys the sense of responsibility the narrator felt toward the children she served.
It describes the narrator's conversations with families about the vaccination schedule.
It suggests that the narrator resented having to walk the last mile to the villages.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence says the cooler 'weighed more than anything inside it' and gives the reason: each name on the list was 'a child waiting.' That extra weight is figurative. It is the weight of knowing that children depend on her. So the sentence shows her sense of responsibility.

A.why: You read the image literally. The text never describes what the cooler is made of. The 'because' clause tells you the weight comes from the children waiting, not from the cooler's materials.

D.why: You misread the tone. The sentence explains why the load felt heavy: children were waiting for her. That shows devotion, not resentment. Nothing in the text suggests she minded the walk.

The following text is from Harold Visser's 1987 short story "The Inspector."

For thirty years Marguerite had climbed beneath the river bridge with a flashlight and a small hammer. She tapped each rivet and listened for the dull note that meant rust. She recorded every hairline crack in a green notebook, and she knew which ones had widened since the winter before. <u>The bridge, in other words, had been the one long conversation of her life.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It sums up the earlier details by casting Marguerite's work as a lifelong relationship.
It reveals that Marguerite spoke aloud to the bridge while she inspected it.
It describes a repair Marguerite made after she discovered rust on a rivet.
It suggests that Marguerite found her years of inspections dull and repetitive.

Thirty years of tapping, listening, and tracking cracks are recast as a 'conversation,' which is a figure for a close, two-way relationship. The sentence summarizes the details and tells you what they meant to her.

D.why: You probably caught the word 'dull,' but in the text it describes the sound that means rust, not her feelings. Calling the bridge 'the one long conversation of her life' shows close attachment, not boredom.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

To recount a disagreement between the narrator and a partner about the most reliable way to count frogs

By the fifth year a highway two miles away is audible, which means the frogs have gone quiet. The last sentence says the quiet 'told me what they would say': the narrator knows the count has dropped without writing it down. So the text exists to show a realization, and the change in what can be heard is how that realization arrives.

B.why: You took the highway as the topic. The text only says the highway could be heard. It never says when or why the road was built or that it damaged anything. The highway shows how quiet the marsh had become.

C.why: You made up a conversation. The partner appears only to show how loud the frogs once were, since the narrator had to shout. No one argues about counting methods anywhere in the text.

D.why: You got the sound backwards. The marsh grew quieter, not noisier. Hearing a distant highway means the frogs had faded. The narrator stops writing numbers because the quiet already gives away the result.

items.stem: Cover the underlined sentence. What job does it do in the text?
choices: It shows that the book mattered to him for more than its music.
It indicates that the book held directions to his home village.
It reveals that he regretted leaving his village at nineteen.
It describes the worn condition of the book's handwritten pages.
items.explanation: The line says the book was 'less a songbook than a map back' to his village. That means it carried his memory of home. The next sentence backs this up: he already knew every tune, so he didn't open it for the notes. The line's job is to show that an object means more than its practical use. Questions about the function of an underlined line often hinge on exactly this kind of meaning.

B.why: You took 'map' literally. The book is a book of fiddle tunes, and the sentence calls it a map only in a figurative sense. Reading it as real directions clashes with everything else the text says about it.
